34: What is the Podio API?
35: The Podio API is a complete programmable interface to all Podio functionality. We currently provide wrappers for PHP, .NET, Ruby, Java, Python, Android and Objective-C which make working with common API operations very simple.
36: What can you do with it?
37: Quite a lot! In fact, the entire Podio frontend is built on the API, and we've exposed it all for you to use too. If you want to build event-driven applications, you have the ability to register webhooks in your Podio apps. There are some sensible rate-limits in place, but if you need us to raise them for your app, get in touch.
38: How do I get started?

24: How to authenticate with Podio API
25: The Podio API uses the OAuth2 protocol for authentication. This allows external apps to request authorization to Podio without having direct access to the user's password. Our API supports different OAuth flows depending on what kind of integration you are making.
26: Before you can use the Podio API you must register your application. Your application is assigned a unique identifier, called "Client ID", together with a "Client Secret". You will need both of these to authenticate. The Client Secret should not be shared with anyone.
27: Authentication flows
28: Podio supports four different ways of autheticating depending on what kind of application you are building:
29: Server-side flow
30: This is the preferred way of authenticating for web apps.
31: Client-side flow
32: Use the client-side flow if your application does not have a server. Examples: Browser extensions, web app running purely in the browser, mobile or desktop applications.
33: Username & password flow
34: Use this flow only if none of the other flows are suitable. It requires the user's username and password to be shared.
35: App authentication flow
36: Use app authentication if you only need to interact with a single Podio app and do not need to authenticate as a specific user. Examples: Automated scripts.
37: All of these authentication methods will provide you with an access token. You will be including this access token in any subsequent requests to the API. You will do this by including an HTTP header with the access token like so:
38: Authorization: OAuth2 ACCESS_TOKEN
39: Where ACCESS_TOKEN should be replaced with the actual access token you have obtained. If you are using one of our client libraries this is handled for you automatically.
40: Token Expiry
41: All tokens received have an associated expiry time. Access Token & refresh Token can be exchanged prior to expiry.
42: Token Expiry Time:
43: Access Token: 8 hours
44: Refresh Token: 28 days
45: Recommended Usage:
46: By default, the access token is valid for 8 hours. So, you need NOT request a new token with each new API call.
47: App Authentication flow, being more secure, is the preferred way of authentication over Username and Password flow.
48: Refreshing expired tokens
49: In addition to the access token, the response also contains a expires_in parameter, and a refresh_token parameter. The value of the expires_in parameter is the number of seconds until the token expires. This is an example of a full response when obtaining an access token:
50: {
51: "access_token": ACCESS_TOKEN,
52: "token_type": "bearer",
53: "expires_in": EXPIRES_IN,
54: "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
55: "scope": GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING,
56: "ref":
57: {
58: "type": "user",
59: "id": USER_ID
60: }
61: }
62: See Scopes & Permissions for details about the value of GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING
63: When the access token expires, you can use the refresh_token to "refresh" your access, and gain another access_token. To use the refresh_token you need to do a POST request to our token-endpoint with the grant_type set to refresh_token:
64: HTTP METHOD: POST
65: URL: https://api.podio.com/oauth/token/v2
66: HEADER: "Content-Type: application/json"
67: BODY:
68: {
69: "grant_type": "refresh_token",
70: "client_id": YOUR_APP_ID,
71: "client_secret": YOUR_APP_SECRET,
72: "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
73: }
74: This request returns the same data as above, and you can continue to do this over and over again, to keep your application authenticated without having to ask the user to re-authenticate.
75: State parameter & Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
76: In order to avoid Cross Site Request Forgery attacks, we recommend you to use an optional state-parameter to pass an identifier, and then validate the state on the response you get from our API.
77: When you make the request to obtain the authorization code include the state parameter like so:
78: https://podio.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_APP_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_URL&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN
79: When the Podio API redirects the user back to your application the state parameter is included and you can validate it:
80: http://YOUR_URL?code=A_CODE_GENERATED_BY_SERVER&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN
81: The state parameter is optional. Any string value can be used.

63: Areas
64: Our API is split up into different areas, that each contains a subset of methods grouped by functionality. You could call each area its own API, but we like to call them areas, because it's just a simple grouping.
65: Core Areas
66: ApplicationsThis area is used to manage application definitions.
67: CommentsComments are made by users on different objects.
68: ContactsEach user has a profile attached, that holds all the personal details of the user.
69: FilesThis area contains all the files that can be uploaded to Podio by end users.
70: HooksHooks are webhooks that can call external sites when certain actions occur in Podio.
71: ItemsItems are entries in an app.
72: OAuth authorizationThis API uses OAuth 2.
73: StatusStatus messages are small texts that the users wishes to share with the other users in a space.
74: TasksTasks are used to track what work has to be done.
75: Other Areas
76: ActionsActions are activities performed by users that does not pertain to one of the core objects in Podio, items, tasks and statuses.
77: AlertsAn alert is a ping from on user to one or more other users.
78: App marketApps and packs can be shared to the app market so they can be installed and used by anyone.
79: BatchThis area contains all the batch operations that the user have executed.
80: CalendarThe calendar is used to get the calendar for a user.
81: ConversationsConversations are private messages exchanged between >=2 users.
82: DevicesMethods needed for supporting external devices like mobile phones and desktop clients.
83: EmailThis area manages emails sent to and received from a user.
84: EmbedsEmbeds are links shared by users in statuses, conversations and comments.
85: FlowsCauses:item.
86: FormsForms can be used to enable direct submission into apps from websites.
87: FriendsAPI for accessing and modifying one's friends in Podio: users that are (or have been in the past) in the same workspace or have interacted directly inside Podio (e.
88: GrantsGrants are single access permissions for specific objects, f.
89: ImporterUsed for importing files into applications, for example, xlsx and xls files.
90: IntegrationsThis API controls the integration supported by Podio "out-of-the-box".
91: LayoutManage application's layout (badge, relationship) definitions.
92: Linked AccountsLinked Accounts represent connections to 3rd-party APIs like Google, Facebook, etc.
93: NotificationsA notification is an information about an event that occured in Podio.
94: OrganizationsThis area holds organizations.
95: QuestionsThe question area makes it possible to attach questions to other objects in Podio.
96: RatingsMany objects can be rated including items and status messages.
97: RecurrenceHandles recurrence for different objects, currently tasks.
98: ReferenceAPI for getting generic information about objects.
99: RemindersReminders are used to remind you about tasks with a due date.
100: SearchThis API makes it possible to search across Podio.
101: Space membersManages membership of spaces.
102: SpacesA space is a work area.
103: StreamThe stream API will supply the different streams.
104: SubscriptionsSubscriptions allows the user to be notified when an object is created, updated, delete, comments added to it or rated.
105: TagsTags are words or short sentences that are used as metadata for objects.
106: UsersThis area holds all the users which just includes basic operations.
107: ViewsViews can be used to limit the items returned when viewing an app.
108: VotingUser-defined voting on an item.
109: WidgetsWidgets are small components that can be installed on an organization, space, app or user.

1: OAuth 2.0 Authentication | Zoho CRM API | V8
2: OAuth 2.0 for V8 APIs - An Overview
3: The Zoho CRM API uses the OAuth 2.0 protocol for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is an industry-standard protocol specification that enables third-party applications (clients) to gain delegated access to protected resources in Zoho via an API.
4: Why should we use OAuth 2.0?
5: How OAuth 2.0 works?
6: Key Terminologies in OAuth 2.0
7: Tokens
8: Why should we use OAuth 2.0?
9: Clients are not required to support password authentication or store user credentials.
10: Clients gain delegated access, i.e., access only to resources authenticated by the user.
11: Users can revoke the client's delegated access anytime.
12: OAuth 2.0 access tokens expire after a set time. If the client faces a security breach, user data will be compromised only until the access token is valid.
13: How OAuth 2.0 works?
14: Key Terminologies in OAuth 2.0
15: The following are some terms you need to know before you start using the Zoho CRM APIs.
16: Protected resources
17: The Zoho CRM resources, such as Leads, Contacts, Deals, etc.
18: Resource server
19: The Zoho CRM server that hosts protected resources.
20: Resource owner
21: Any end-user of your account, who can grant access to the protected resources.
22: Client
23: An application that sends requests to the resource server to access the protected resources on behalf of the end-user.
24: Client ID
25: The consumer key generated from the connected application.
26: Client Secret
27: The consumer secret generated from the connected application.
28: Authentication server
29: Authorization server provides the necessary credentials (such as Access and Refresh tokens) to the client. In this case, it will be the Zoho CRM authorization server.
30: Authentication code
31: The authorization server creates a temporary token and sends it to the client via the browser. The client will send this code to the authorization server to obtain access and refresh tokens.
32: Tokens
33: Access Token
34: A token that is sent to the resource server to access the protected resources of the user. The Access token provides secure and temporary access to the protected resources and is used by the applications to make requests to the connected app. Each access token will be valid only for an hour and can be used only for the set of operations that are described in the scope.
35: Refresh Token
36: A token that can be used to obtain new access tokens. This token has an unlimited lifetime until it is revoked by the end-user.
37: Important
38: User Access Token must be kept confidential since it provides access to protected resources. Do NOT expose your Access Token anywhere in public forums, public repositories or on your website's client-side code like HTML or JavaScript. Exposing it to the public may lead to data theft, loss or corruption.

185: Product Understanding
186: What is Zoho MCP?
187: Zoho MCP is a product built around the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standardized interface that allows AI agents to interact with business software. With Zoho MCP, you can create MCP Servers that expose tools, actions, and contextual data from Zoho apps in a way AI agents can understand and act upon, regardless of which LLM they use.
188: While MCP is the open protocol that defines how agents communicate with business systems, Zoho MCP provides the infrastructure, configuration UI, security, and integrations needed to implement it quickly and securely within the Zoho ecosystem (and beyond). In short:
189: MCP is the protocol
190: Zoho MCP is the product that lets you stand up agent-ready endpoints, making Zoho apps executable by AI agents.
191: How is MCP different from chatbot builders or automation tools?
192: Zoho MCP isn’t a chatbot builder or an automation tool, it’s the execution layer that enables AI agents to take real action. Traditional chatbot builders focus on conversation flow. Automation tools execute predefined, rule-based workflows. Zoho MCP takes a different approach: it exposes your apps' tools, actions, and business context through a standardized protocol, so AI agents (powered by any LLM) can turn natural language into real outcomes.
193: While LLMs handle intent understanding, MCP enables agents to:
194: Access structured data (like deals, meetings, or tasks)
195: Trigger product-level actions (like sending invoices or creating records)
196: Coordinate multi-step workflows without rigid scripts
197: Unlike chatbots that reply or automation tools that need manual configuration, Zoho MCP lets agents operate your apps directly, securely, and autonomously.
198: Are AI Agents and Zoho MCP the same?
199: No, AI agents and Zoho MCP are not the same.
200: AI agents are intelligent systems often powered by LLMs like GPT or Claude , that interpret natural language and act on user intent. Zoho MCP is a product built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that exposes structured tools, data, and actions from Zoho apps in a way agents can use. It allows developers to create MCP servers that agents connect to via an MCP client
201: In this relationship:
202: The agent handles the intelligence and interpretation.
203: MCP provides the execution interface (what actions are available, how they work, and what’s allowed).
204: Think of MCP as the infrastructure layer and agents as the brains and operators.
205: Zoho MCP doesn’t make agents smarter, it makes them more capable of acting.
206: What kind of AI agents can I build with MCP?
207: You can build task-based, goal-based, or autonomous agents. Agents can be reactive or autonomous, depending on your goals.
208: Examples include:
209: A sales assistant that schedules meetings and sends proposals
210: A support agent that triages tickets and notifies teams
211: A project bot that tracks tasks and updates timelines
212: Technical
213: Do I need technical or coding experience to use MCP?
214: Not at all. Through its UI, you can configure MCP servers, define tools, and manage authentication with minimal code. It provides a low-code way to expose Zoho app functionality to AI agents.
215: What models, such as GPT or Claude, are supported?
216: Zoho MCP is completely model-agnostic. It doesn't connect to or depend on any specific LLM. Instead, it exposes a standardized interface that any AI agent, powered by any LLM, can call through an MCP client.
217: Whether you’re using GPT, Claude, a fine-tuned model, or an open-source LLM, as long as your agent speaks the MCP protocol, it can securely access tools, actions, and data across your Zoho apps.
218: Business Impact
219: How will this benefit my team or company?
220: Zoho MCP dramatically cuts time spent toggling between apps, performing manual tasks, or managing workflows. Agents streamline execution, so your team focuses on decisions, not distractions. It boosts productivity, speeds up response times, and minimizes errors. It provides the structured tools, APIs, and secure access needed for agents to turn interpreted intent into real actions - across CRM, Calendar, Books, and more.
221: While the LLM interprets natural language, MCP is what lets the agent act on it - by exposing data, context, and business logic in a standardized, secure way. So instead of just responding to users, MCP-enabled agents can actually get work done
222: What kinds of workflows can MCP automate?
223: Everything from lead follow-ups and internal notifications to deal tracking and project updates. If it’s a routine task that lives across Zoho apps—or even third-party tools—MCP agents can handle it with context and precision.
224: Common workflows include:
225: Lead follow-ups and meeting scheduling
226: Sales proposals and contract approvals
227: Ticket escalations and support routing
228: Internal updates and stakeholder alerts, and more
229: Access & Security
230: Who can access the MCP playground?
231: New users can sign up and start using MCP immediately, while Zoho users, developers, and partners can log in to access the MCP playground.
232: Is MCP secure?
233: Yes. MCP follows Zoho’s enterprise-grade security protocols. All data access and agent actions are governed by strict access controls, encrypted data handling, and audit trails, ensuring safe, compliant execution.
234: How does MCP handle authentication and permissions?
235: Agents operate under user-level permissions, so they can only perform actions that the user is authorized to do. Zoho supports OAuth to ensure secure identity management.
236: Integration & Compatibility
237: Which Zoho apps does MCP work with today?
238: MCP integrates with many Zoho apps, including CRM, Mail, Calendar, Desk, Cliq, Projects, and WorkDrive. It leverages existing APIs and standard actions, so your agents can operate across tools natively.
239: Does MCP support third-party tools like Asana or Twilio?
240: Yes, you can extend agent actions to tools like Asana, Twilio, OneDrive, Notion, and more. MCP is designed to be flexible for multi-app workflows. With MCP, you can connect to 500+ third party apps. For any unsupported apps, please raise a request to support@zohomcp.com

18: API keys are best used for scripts and simple integrations that are internal to

21: Getting an API key
22: API keys can be created and managed in your Close account under Settings → Developer → API Keys.
23: API keys are scoped to a particular user/organization combination and can be generated and deleted in the Settings page. See API Keys & OAuth for more information.
24: Perform API calls with API key
25: API keys use
26: HTTP Basic client side authentication.
27: Basic authentication is a simple authentication scheme built into the HTTP
28: protocol. To use it, send your HTTP requests with an Authorization header that
29: contains the word Basic followed by a space and a base64-encoded string composed
30: of an api key followed by a colon. The API key acts as the username and the
31: password is always empty.
32: cURL example
33: Example cURL request with an api key.
34: curl https://api.close.com/api/v1/me/ -u yourapikey:
35: Notice the ’:’ at the end of the api key. This is used because the key is sent
36: as the username with a blank password.
37: GET /api/v1/me/ HTTP/1.1
38: Authorization: Basic eW91cmFwaWtleTo=
39: Host: api.close.com
40: This results in the header Authorization: Basic eW91cmFwaWtleTo= sent with the
41: request as base64-encoded string yourapikey: is eW91cmFwaWtleTo=
42: API Base URL: https://api.close.com/api/v1

245: AI credits & shared limitsIncluded per user each month and pooled across your team, up to 10,000 on Essentials, 15,000 on Growth, and 20,000 on Scale. Credits refresh monthly and do not roll over. Additional credits are available.

249: Close pricing FAQs
250: Still deciding? Our team can help you pick a plan, plan a migration, or set up your first workflows.
251: Talk to Sales
252: How much does Close cost?
253: Close costs $9/month for Solo (one user), $35 per user/month for Essentials, $99 per user/month for Growth, and $139 per user/month for Scale, billed annually. Billed monthly, the plans are $19, $49, $109, and $149. Calling and SMS are billed separately based on usage, and every plan includes monthly AI credits.
254: Which Close plan is right for my team?
255: Solo is for one seller working alone. Essentials is for small teams that need shared leads, tasks, reporting, and Local Presence. Growth is for teams that want to make more calls and automate follow-up, with Power Dialer, Workflows, and AI Playbooks. Scale is for high-volume calling teams that need Predictive Dialer, Live Call Coaching, and advanced permissions. You can start on any plan and upgrade as your team and call volume grow.
256: Is Close free?
257: Close doesn’t have a free plan, but you can try it free for 14 days with no credit card. The trial includes calling and AI credits, so you can call real leads and try Chloe and AI Agents before you pay. After the trial, plans start at $9/month for Solo, billed annually.
258: What happens when my free trial ends?
259: If you choose a plan, you keep working in Close without interruption. If you don’t, your account pauses and your data stays available for a limited period before it’s deleted.
260: Are there any costs beyond the plan price?
261: Yes. Calling and SMS usage fees are not included in plan costs; you only pay for what you use. Most outbound calls cost about $0.02 per minute, phone numbers start at about $1/month, and SMS rates vary by country. AI usage beyond your included monthly credits is billed separately. AI Call Assistant is an optional add-on at $50/month per account plus $0.02 per recorded minute.
262: Do I need a separate phone system or sales dialer with Close?
263: No. Close includes built-in calling on every plan, so you can make and receive calls without switching tools. Growth adds the Power Dialer to call through lead lists automatically, and Scale includes the Predictive Dialer for high-volume outbound calling. Calls are logged in Close automatically. Calling minutes and phone numbers are billed separately.
264: How do AI credits work?
265: AI credits pay for AI that does work for you: AI Agents, AI Enrichment, Auto Updates, AI steps in Workflows, and Chloe chats beyond your weekly allowance. Lead summaries, email thread summaries, AI Notetaker, AI Rewrite, and Suggested Actions don’t use credits. Each plan includes credits per user every month (500 on Solo; 1,000, 1,500, or 2,000 per user on Essentials, Growth, and Scale), pooled across your team up to 10,000, 15,000, or 20,000. Credits reset monthly, don’t roll over, and you can buy more anytime.
266: Which plans include Chloe and AI Agents?
267: Every Close plan, including Solo, includes Chloe and AI Agents. Chloe is your AI assistant: ask about your leads, pipeline, or last call, or have her take action in Close. AI Agents work for you on ongoing jobs like calling and qualifying new leads. Growth and Scale add AI Playbooks, Auto Updates, and AI steps in Workflows.
268: Can I connect Close to ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI tools?
269: Yes. Every Close plan includes access to our MCP server, which lets you connect compatible AI assistants and agents to your CRM. Use tools like ChatGPT and Claude to access sales information, analyze conversations, update records, and take supported actions in Close. Available features and setup requirements vary by AI tool.
270: Learn more about Close MCP
271: Does Close include API access?
272: Yes. Close provides a REST API for building custom integrations, connecting your applications, and automating sales processes. API requests are subject to rate limits, but Close does not have a published daily API request quota or separate per-request API fees.
273: Explore the Close API
274: Does Close have API rate limits?
275: Yes. Close uses endpoint-specific rate limits to maintain reliability. Many commonly used endpoints support high request volumes, allowing businesses to build integrations, AI agents, and automations without a daily API request quota. Limits vary by endpoint.
276: View the API documentation
277: Can I change or cancel my plan anytime?
278: Yes. Monthly plans can be upgraded, downgraded, or canceled anytime. Annual plans can be upgraded during the term, and downgrades or cancellations take effect at the end of the term. You can add users as your team grows, and new seats are prorated. Every new purchase comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee.
279: Can I bring my existing CRM data into Close?
280: Yes. Close offers free migration help for standard moves from HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, and other CRMs, and you can import data yourself with built-in importers or a spreadsheet. Complex migrations, such as multiple systems, heavy cleanup, or custom requirements, may include professional services fees.
281: Do I need to talk to sales?
282: No. You can sign up, start a trial, pick a plan, and set up your team without talking to sales. Our team is available if you want help choosing a plan, planning a migration, or setting up Workflows.

286: About Close
287: Close is the AI CRM for small and growing businesses that want to sell more and scale faster. With built-in calling, email, SMS, pipeline management, and sales automation, your team has everything it needs to sell in one place. Chloe, your AI assistant, helps you take action, while AI agents qualify leads, follow up, and handle sales work for you. Win more customers without the complexity of traditional CRM software. evidence.observation: quote: The DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG and DEFAULT_TARGET_DEV_HUB tokens are resolved dynamically on every tool call, not pinned when the server starts. They track whatever the default org resolves to for the working directory a tool operates in, so switching your default org (or working in a directory with a different local default) changes which org these tokens allow. This mirrors how the sf CLI resolves the default target-org when you don't pass --target-org. If you want to lock the server to a fixed set of orgs regardless of the current default, pass explicit usernames or aliases to --orgs instead of the DEFAULT_TARGET_* tokens.

evidence.observation: quote: The HubSpot Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enables AI assistants and Large Language Models to securely interact with your HubSpot CRM data through natural conversation. By implementing the Model Context Protocol standard, this remote server acts as a bridge between AI systems and HubSpot’s APIs, allowing for intelligent automation and insights without requiring users to understand complex API structures.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: For developers, the remote HubSpot MCP server provides secure, granular access to HubSpot CRM data through AI agents and third-party applications, and allows teams to build custom workflows, automate reporting, and integrate HubSpot context into third-party applications. For end-users, it creates a more streamlined, simpler way to query their HubSpot data using natural language.

evidence.observation: quote: The HubSpot MCP server documented on this page is separate from the developer MCP server. The developer MCP server helps developers build apps and CMS content assets locally on HubSpot’s developer platform. In contrast, the HubSpot MCP server is intended for making requests to an account’s CRM data, similar to using HubSpot’s APIs.

evidence_rules:
# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.
